explain.say: On 28 June 1914, in Sarajevo, a nineteen-year-old Bosnian Serb named Gavrilo Princip shot Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to Austria-Hungary, and his wife Sophie. Six weeks later most of Europe's great powers were at war. Look at the web of alliances. One pulled thread could tug them all.

explain.say: Why was Europe so ready to explode? See the long-term causes. Britain and Germany raced to build battleships, the great powers kept huge armies, empires clashed over Morocco, and Serbian nationalism threatened Austria-Hungary's rule over South Slavs. Which cause feels most like dry wood waiting for a match?

explain.say: Now the July Crisis, day by day. Germany gave Austria a blank cheque, a promise of full support. Austria sent Serbia a harsh ultimatum and declared war on 28 July. Russia mobilised to protect Serbia, and Germany declared war on Russia and then France. Watch the dates speed up. Where could someone have stopped it?

events.label: Ultimatum
events.note: Austria makes harsh demands of Serbia.

explain.say: Look at the map. Germany's Schlieffen Plan aimed to beat France fast by marching through neutral Belgium, then turn east against Russia. On 4 August German troops entered Belgium, and Britain, which had promised in 1839 to protect Belgian neutrality, declared war. Why did a plan made years earlier leave so little time for talks?

Now the debate. In 1961 Fritz Fischer argued Germany sought war to dominate Europe. In 2012 Christopher Clark called the leaders sleepwalkers, with risks taken in Vienna, Belgrade, Saint Petersburg and Paris as well as Berlin. Great thinking. Exam tip: separate long-term causes from the decisions of July 1914.

faq.q: What caused the First World War?
faq.a: Long-term causes included militarism, two rival alliance blocs, imperial rivalry and nationalism, especially in the Balkans. The trigger was the assassination of Franz Ferdinand, followed by the July Crisis of 1914 in which governments chose war.

faq.q: Why did the assassination of Franz Ferdinand lead to a world war?
faq.a: Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia and, with German backing, declared war on it. Russia mobilised to support Serbia, Germany declared war on Russia and France, and Germany's invasion of Belgium brought Britain in. Alliances and war plans turned a local conflict into a general one.
On 5 and 6 July 1914 Germany promised Austria-Hungary full support in whatever action it took against Serbia. Historians see it as a key step that encouraged Austria to risk war.

faq.q: Was Germany to blame for the First World War?
faq.a: Fritz Fischer, in 1961, argued Germany bore the main responsibility because it sought European dominance. Christopher Clark, in 2012, argued responsibility was shared among several powers that took risks. Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles placed blame on Germany and its allies.

Germany's war plan to defeat France quickly by invading through Belgium, then turn to fight Russia. Its strict timetable pushed Germany to act fast once Russia mobilised, and the invasion of Belgium brought Britain into the war.
asks: Why did Britain join the war?

facts: Franz Ferdinand was assassinated in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914.
Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on 28 July 1914.
Britain declared war on Germany on 4 August 1914 after the invasion of Belgium.

quiz.say: What brought Britain into the war in August 1914?
quiz.why: Britain had guaranteed Belgian neutrality in 1839 and declared war when Germany invaded.

wrong.1: The assassination began the crisis but did not directly involve Britain.
wrong.2: Germany declared war on Russia; Russia's mobilisation came first, but that was not Britain's reason.

quiz.say: Which historian called the leaders of 1914 sleepwalkers?
quiz.why: Clark's 2012 book The Sleepwalkers stressed shared responsibility.

wrong.1: Fischer argued that Germany carried the main blame.
wrong.2: Hobsbawm wrote broad histories of the period but not this book.
